title: Durham's Lunceford arrangements
summary: He lists Harlem Shout, Lunceford Special, Bird of Paradise, Running a Temperature, Hitting the Bottle and Avalon, and contrasts his writing with Sy Oliver's.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Let's just talk a little more about Lunceford, though, now. What were the main things you arranged for him?
I made his Harlem Shout.
Yes.
That's that Harlem Shout album. And I made his Lunceford Special album. And I did numbers like Bird of Paradise.
That was the one -- that was Duke's tune.
Yeah.
That was the one you worked on with -- didn't you have to work with Eddie Wilcox on that?
With the piano?
Yeah.
Yeah, he could play. And I did a lot of horn work, Running a Temperature, and --
Oh, Boy?
Oh, Boy, and Hitting the Bottle and --
Avalon?

Avalon, and (inaudible). And I wrote one in there he called Oh, Eddie. These originals, because we made a lot of arrangements. Well, Running A Temperature and those wasn't arrangements, but a lot of those others --
(Inaudible) you did?
Yeah. And I can't think of all of the rest of them.
So all this time, the -- you and Sy Oliver were both sort of writing arrangements.
Yeah.
Well, that was a good idea, in a way, because there was a contrast, wasn't there?
Yeah, uh-huh.
You know, the styles were different.
Yeah. And then I did Swinging on a , the same thing Earl Hines did.
Oh, yes, yes.

I could name a lot of them. But I was taking up a lot of times, trying to help the guys voicing that six-part. They didn't have any knowledge in that. Then I wrote a lot of things where we used five saxes, too. But I used Dan Grisson on the sax.
Yeah.
See, and that was, like, Honey, Keep Your Mind on Me, and a few other things.
Yeah, so --
If you notice close, he's playing saxophone on that, the singer.
